note: Rule catalogue. Matching is in scan_migrations.py (one function per rule id); this file holds what each rule means. versions: the engine versions the rule applies to ('*' for all, or a range like '<11').

PG-INDEX-LOCKS-WRITES.effect: CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock on {table}: inserts, updates and deletes wait until the index is built
PG-INDEX-LOCKS-WRITES.rewrite: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own non-transactional migration (Alembic: with op.get_context().autocommit_block(), postgresql_concurrently=True)

PG-CONCURRENTLY-IN-TRANSACTION.effect: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block: the migration fails
PG-CONCURRENTLY-IN-TRANSACTION.rewrite: Run it outside the migration transaction (autocommit_block, atomic = False, disable_ddl_transaction!)

PG-TYPE-CHANGE-REWRITE.effect: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites {table} under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock: reads and writes wait for the whole rewrite
PG-TYPE-CHANGE-REWRITE.rewrite: Add a new column of the new type, backfill it in batches, dual-write, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release

TYPE-NARROWING.effect: {from} to {to} narrows the column: values that don't fit are rounded, truncated or rejected
TYPE-NARROWING.rewrite: Check every value fits first (SELECT count(*) WHERE col <> col::newtype), convert explicitly with USING, and keep the old column until verified

PG-ADD-COLUMN-DEFAULT.effect: ADD COLUMN with a default rewrites {table} when the default is volatile, or on PostgreSQL before 11
PG-ADD-COLUMN-DEFAULT.rewrite: Add the column without a default, set the default separately, backfill in batches

PG-SET-NOT-NULL-SCAN.effect: SET NOT NULL scans all of {table} under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
PG-SET-NOT-NULL-SCAN.rewrite: ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a later migration; then SET NOT NULL (PostgreSQL 12+ skips the scan)

PG-FK-VALIDATE.effect: ADD FOREIGN KEY validates every row of {table} while holding locks on both tables
PG-FK-VALIDATE.rewrite: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a separate migration

PG-NO-LOCK-TIMEOUT.effect: DDL runs with no lock_timeout: if a long query holds {table}, the migration waits and every later query queues behind it
PG-NO-LOCK-TIMEOUT.rewrite: SET lock_timeout = '5s' (and a statement_timeout) at the start of each migration, or in env.py, and retry on timeout

DROP-TABLE.effect: DROP TABLE {table} deletes the table and its data
DROP-TABLE.rewrite: Rename or archive first; drop in a later release after a backup

DROP-COLUMN.effect: DROP COLUMN {column} deletes the column's data in {table}
DROP-COLUMN.rewrite: Stop reading and writing it first (one release), back it up, then drop

TRUNCATE.rewrite: Delete only what must go, with a WHERE clause and a backup

DML-WITHOUT-WHERE.effect: {verb} on {table} with no WHERE changes every row
DML-WITHOUT-WHERE.rewrite: Add a WHERE clause and run it in batches

BACKFILL-UNBATCHED.effect: One UPDATE over {table} in a single transaction: row locks on every matching row until it commits, and a long-running transaction
BACKFILL-UNBATCHED.rewrite: Backfill in batches (WHERE id BETWEEN ...) outside the schema migration, committing each batch

IRREVERSIBLE.effect: The down migration is {state}: this migration can't be rolled back
IRREVERSIBLE.rewrite: Write a down that restores what the up changed, or mark the migration irreversible on purpose and say how to recover

RENAME-WHILE-READ.effect: Renaming {table}.{column} breaks code that still uses the old name during the deploy
RENAME-WHILE-READ.rewrite: Expand and contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one in a later release

DROP-WHILE-READ.effect: Dropping {table}.{column} breaks code that still reads it
DROP-WHILE-READ.rewrite: Remove the code that reads it in an earlier release

NOT-NULL-WHILE-WRITTEN-WITHOUT.effect: {table}.{column} becomes NOT NULL while code still inserts rows without it
NOT-NULL-WHILE-WRITTEN-WITHOUT.rewrite: Ship code that always sends the column (or a server default) first; make it NOT NULL in a later release

ALEMBIC-MULTIPLE-HEADS.effect: The migration chain has more than one head: {heads}
ALEMBIC-MULTIPLE-HEADS.rewrite: Merge the heads (alembic merge) before deploying

MYSQL-COPY-ALTER.effect: This ALTER can't run in place (ALGORITHM=COPY or a column type change): {table} is copied and writes are blocked
MYSQL-COPY-ALTER.rewrite: Use an online schema change tool (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change), or split the change

MYSQL-DDL-AUTOCOMMIT.effect: MySQL commits each DDL statement: a failure halfway leaves the migration half applied
MYSQL-DDL-AUTOCOMMIT.rewrite: One DDL statement per migration, or make each step idempotent

PG-UNIQUE-CONSTRAINT-LOCK.effect: ADD CONSTRAINT UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY builds its index on {table} under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock: reads and writes wait until the index is built
PG-UNIQUE-CONSTRAINT-LOCK.rewrite: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own non-transactional migration, then ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX

PG-CHECK-VALIDATE.effect: ADD CHECK scans every row of {table} under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to validate it
PG-CHECK-VALIDATE.rewrite: ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a separate migration

DELETE-ROWS.effect: DELETE on {table} removes the matching rows, and nothing in the migration keeps a copy
DELETE-ROWS.rewrite: Copy the rows to a backup table (or export them) in the same migration before deleting, and restore them in the down migration

VALUE-RENAME-WHILE-READ.effect: UPDATE renames the value '{old}' of {table}.{column} to '{new}': code still keyed on '{old}' (the previous release, during a rolling deploy) stops matching
VALUE-RENAME-WHILE-READ.rewrite: Expand and contract: ship code that accepts both values first, rename the value in a later release, then drop the old value from the code

MIGRATION-READS-FILES.effect: The migration reads files from the repository at run time ({paths}); when they move or are deleted, the step does nothing or fails on every database built later
MIGRATION-READS-FILES.rewrite: Put the data the step needs in the migration itself (a literal list or VALUES), or fail loudly when the files are missing
